Received gifts lead into a prayer for understanding rather than a claim to rank

Verses 3–14 list gifts already given: choosing, redemption, an inheritance, the Spirit. The prayer in verses 17–19 asks for nothing new to be added. It asks that they see what they have. Verse 18 pictures the heart with eyes that need light. Three things are to be known. The verse names two: the hope of his calling and his rich inheritance. Verse 19 names the third: the greatness of his power toward believers.
Former outsiders become members of one household through the removal of hostility

Verse 12 lists what the Gentile readers lacked. They were apart from Christ, shut out of Israel, strangers to the covenants. Verse 14 says Christ broke down the wall of hostility. Verse 19 restates their position with the same kind of words. They are no longer strangers and foreigners. They are fellow citizens and members of God’s household. Verse 20 turns household into house, built on the apostles and prophets.
The prisoner's task serves shared inheritance and leads into prayer for strength

Verse 3 speaks of a mystery made known by revelation. Verse 5 says other generations did not know it as now. Verse 6 states its content in three words that begin “fellow.” The Gentiles are fellow heirs, fellow members, and fellow partakers of the promise. Each word gives them a full share with Israel’s believers. The means is named at the end: through the good news. Verse 1 shows the cost to Paul: he is a prisoner for these Gentiles.
One body needs different gifts and conduct that allows its members to grow

Verses 22–24 speak of putting off the old man and putting on the new. Verse 25 gives the first plain case, and it starts with “therefore.” They are to put away falsehood and speak truth with a neighbor. The reason is not a rule about lying in general. It is that “we are members of one another.” The phrase recalls the body in verse 16, where each part supplies. A lie between members harms the body both belong to.
Shared submission leads into unequal household roles measured against Christ's self-giving love

Verse 21 tells all of them to submit to one another. Verses 22–24 then address wives, and verses 25–33 address husbands at greater length. Verse 25 gives the husband’s part a measure: love as Christ loved the assembly. That love is defined by an act: he “gave himself up for her.” Verse 28 adds a second measure: husbands should love wives as their own bodies. Verse 29 says no one hates his own flesh but feeds it.
Household commands lead into shared resistance supported by peace and prayer

Verse 11 says to put on armor against the devil’s schemes. Verse 12 explains who the fight is against, and who it is not. It is not against flesh and blood. That excludes human opponents, even the ones who chained Paul (verse 20). The enemies named are powers, rulers of darkness, and spiritual forces. The armor fits that fight: truth, righteousness, peace, faith, and God’s word. Verse 18 adds prayer for all the saints.
